---
title: "Project history"
description: "How the project started, and the original plan."
---

Pete's PDF to MD started in February 2026 as a way to get long, structured PDF documents into AI tools without losing their structure. The first prototype used Swift and Apple's PDF tools, which only ran on macOS, so the converter was rewritten in Python with PyMuPDF to work on both Macs and PCs, with an Electron window added on top.

That version worked well, but everyone who downloaded it had to install Python and two add-ons from Terminal first, and the app was a 110 MB download. In October 2026 a review of [pdf-inspector](https://github.com/firecrawl/pdf-inspector), a PDF library written in Rust, showed a way out. Version 1.0 is the result: the converter was rewritten in Rust on top of pdf-inspector, every cleanup rule from the Python version was carried over and checked against the same test documents, and the window moved from Electron to Tauri. The app is now a single 6 MB download with nothing to install, and it converts documents 4 to 15 times faster.

The plan below, written at the start, is kept for the record. Most of it happened: the three output files, the split modes, the Electron interface and the right-click actions all shipped by v0.7.0. One thing changed along the way: the project chose PyMuPDF instead of Marker for extraction, to keep the app small and fast.

For what changed in each release, see the [Changelog](changelog.qmd).

## Looking ahead

- A Windows version of the 1.0 app.
- A search box to find sections and text in a converted document.
- Better handling of the remaining hard cases: charts with many short cells, and side-by-side boxes on slides.

---

## The original plan (February 2026)

### Goal

Build a standalone app that converts PDF to Markdown accurately and can split output into smaller sub-documents for LLM use.

### Options

1. Build final app immediately, with all features in one flow.
   - Pros: faster path to a single distributable app.
   - Cons: slower iteration on extraction quality; harder to debug heading logic.
2. Build a focused Phase 1 prototype for heading outline + split points, then integrate into final app.
   - Pros: fastest way to validate accuracy and splitting strategy on real PDFs.
   - Cons: one temporary CLI/prototype step before full UI packaging.

### Recommendation

Use Option 2.

Phase 1 should produce three artifacts from each PDF:

- `outline.json`: ordered headings with level, page, and confidence.
- `outline.md`: human-readable heading tree.
- `segments.json`: section boundaries for sub-document generation.

Once this is reliable on your sample PDFs, wire it into the Electron app as:

- `--extract-outline`
- `--split-by-headings`

### Proposed milestones

1. Add a cross-platform CLI runner for local testing (`scripts/phase1.js` + `scripts/extract_outline.py`).
2. Integrate Marker as the extraction backend and normalize heading output.
3. Add heuristic cleanup (merge wrapped headers, drop false positives).
4. Add split-export modes (`single`, `By Major Heading`, `Sections`) with mode-specific output folders.
5. Integrate same pipeline into Electron UI.

### Acceptance criteria for Phase 1

1. Heading hierarchy is readable and mostly correct on at least 3 different PDFs.
2. Split files preserve heading context and are <= configurable target size.
3. Output is deterministic across repeated runs on same input.

### UI to-do

1. Add right-click actions for each section item: "Open in folder" and "Open in default program".
2. When selecting a different section, reset the section content pane scroll position to the top.
3. v0.7.0: Add Shift-click multi-select in Sections and a merge action to combine selected sections into one merged output.
